elements.content: The day started around 10 AM when I finally woke up. Pratiksha had already been waiting for me because we were supposed to start our walking challenge together. But there was one small problem—Saturday is usually my leg day, and I really didn't want to skip it. So naturally, before attempting to walk 50,000 steps, I decided to train legs at the gym first. Pratiksha wasn't very happy with this decision, but after brushing and eating some kanda poha, bananas and rice, I left for the gym around 11 AM. The workout went really well. It was a proper, successful leg day, and I finished around 1:30 PM after stretching and packing my things. At that point, my legs were feeling great. They had absolutely no idea what was coming later.

It all started with a slightly crazy idea. Pratiksha and I had decided to walk 50,000 steps in a single day. And unlike what you might expect, 30,000 was never the original target. The target was always 50,000. From the moment we started walking, we were aiming for it. Somewhere in our minds, 50,000 steps sounded difficult but achievable. We were confident. Maybe a little too confident.

elements.content: After the gym, I still had another thing to do. The next day, Sunday, I had plans with my office friends at Second Nature in Bandra, so I went for a haircut and beard trim. I reached the salon around 2–2:15 PM and left around 3–3:15 PM. By the time I reached home, it was already around 3:30 PM. I took a bath, had lunch... which included rice, four eggs and other food....washed the dishes and got ready for the walk. By around 4 PM, I was ready. Pratiksha, however, was sleepy. After waiting for me the entire day, she had almost given up on the walking plan and was ready to sleep. But I wasn't ready to cancel it. I packed my bag with the essentials (my cap, water bottle, bandana, phone and waterproof phone cover) and somehow managed to convince her to get up.
Finally, around 4:15 PM, we left home. The 50,000-step challenge had officially begun.

elements.html: 4:15 PM — The Walk Begins

elements.content: We started from Jakat Naka and began walking towards Boling through Patil Ali. There wasn't a very complicated route or detailed plan. We simply knew we had to keep walking. We continued towards Navapur and eventually reached the famous Vada Pav wali Aaji. Along the way, we also took plenty of pictures, talked, walked through familiar roads and enjoyed seeing everything at a much slower pace than usual. Somewhere between Navapur and Rajodi, we took a small break, drank some water and clicked a few more photos. By the time we reached the intersection that leads towards Rajodi, it had started getting dark. Instead of continuing towards Rajodi, we decided it was better to turn back and start making our way home. We still had a lot of walking  left to do.....😮‍💨

The Coconut Water Break 🥥

While walking back, we found a Nariyal Pani wali aunty and both of us immediately got two coconut waters. After walking for hours, that coconut water felt unbelievably refreshing. For a few minutes, the tiredness disappeared and everything felt better again. Of course, we were still only halfway through our journey.

elements.content:
The Frog Incident 🐸

As we both continued walking, Pratiksha was walking a few steps ahead of me on the left side of the road while I simply followed behind her. At one point, a frog jumped from the right side of the road and landed between us. I assumed it would make one more jump in the same direction and leave the road. That seemed logical. But apparently, the frog had different plans. Instead of jumping away, it turned towards me, looked directly at me and jumped towards my leg. I was completely shocked. I jumped in the most ridiculous way possible and immediately ran while trying to control my laughter. I genuinely did not expect my biggest enemy during a 20-kilometre walk to be a frog. The frog definitely won that round.

elements.content: After walking for some more time, we started getting properly hungry. Our parents had gone to a pooja at one of their friends' places, so we called them to check if they were having dinner there. Luckily, they had already eaten, which meant we could eat outside. I found an egg stall and had two boiled eggs along with a two-egg omelette. Pratiksha found a dosa stall, and we both had a masala dosa. We were finally full and satisfied, and after resting for a while, continued walking again.
Efficiency. Or cruelty. Depends on who you ask.

elements.content: By this point, Pratiksha was starting to get exhausted. To make things even better, she had also trained her legs earlier that day with a home workout, probably involving squats and other leg exercises. So both of us had somehow trained our legs and then decided to spend the rest of the evening walking for kilometres. Eventually, we stopped near a banana shop and bought four bananas—two for me and two for her. Pratiksha wanted to sit down and eat them, but I told her we could walk while eating and save some time

elements.content:
Reality Check

Eventually, around 9:30 PM, we reached MHADA. By then, we had been walking for hours, our legs were tired and we genuinely felt like we had covered a huge distance. Then we checked our step counts.

Around 25,000 steps.

That was when reality finally hit us. We had been aiming for 50,000 steps the entire day, but after more than five hours of walking, it was already 9:30 PM and we were only halfway there. Another 25,000 steps meant walking for several more hours, and suddenly the original target didn't seem as achievable as it had earlier in the day. So right there in MHADA, we changed the plan. 50,000 steps was no longer the target. 30,000 steps was. Honestly, it felt like the most sensible decision we had made all day.

elements.content:
The Final 5,000 Steps

We still needed around 5,000 more steps to reach our new target. So instead of going home, we walked around MHADA for another 40–50 minutes. By now, Pratiksha was completely exhausted. Her legs had reached their limit, so she waited near a flower stall while I took her phone and walked ahead to complete some extra steps. After covering some distance, I came back, and we carefully calculated how much more we needed to walk. The plan was simple now: walk just enough so that by the time we reached home, we would complete 30,000 steps. And finally, we started our last stretch towards home.

elements.content: We reached home with 30,000 steps                  completed. Strava showed around 20 kilometres walked—our longest walk ever. After a full leg workout, hours of walking, coconut water, bananas, eggs, dosa and one unexpected frog attack, we had actually completed the challenge. We were exhausted, but also relieved and happy. Pratiksha took a shower first while I was outside doing my scrub and skincare. Then I took my shower, and both of us finally freshened up and slept peacefully. The next day, I had plans with my office friends at Second Nature. But that was tomorrow's problem. For now, the challenge was over.

The Real Reason why We Did This 👓

The funniest part is that the main reason behind this entire adventure was actually a Lenskart challenge called Run for Frame. The challenge promised a free frame worth up to ₹2,000 if we completed the required steps. So we walked 30,000 steps. Around 20 kilometres. And after all that... They still charged us ₹800. But honestly, I got a ₹3,000 frame for ₹800, so I guess it wasn't a bad deal after all.

elements.content: We started the day with a target of 50,000 steps and ended it with 30,000. Somewhere along the way, though, it became much more than just a step challenge. It became a long Saturday adventure with my sister—full of tired legs, random conversations, familiar roads, coconut water, bananas, street food, darkness, laughter and one very aggressive frog. The frame was nice. The memory was better.
